hero.lead: A nation of 9,500 on low coral atolls, among the smallest on earth, where fewer than one in ten have safely managed drinking water and the World Bank finances its harbours, fisheries and resilience.

register.name: Second Climate and Disaster Resilience DPF
register.detail: World Bank · Grant · Announced in Funafuti 1 March 2025 · Second in a series of two operations
register.note: ADB counts a $7 million World Bank grant in 2025 as cofinancing for subprogram 1 of its Supporting Public Sector Management Reform Program
register.text: Budget support from the World Bank to help the government assess, monitor, report on and manage climate finance, set aside more funding to respond to disasters, speed up the delivery of emergency supplies and build to standards that withstand natural disasters. Disasters cost Tuvalu almost 7 percent of its GDP each year, according to the World Bank, so funds set aside in advance protect public spending on the seven standards.

register.name: Maritime Investment in Climate Resilient Operations II, additional financing
register.text: Harbours and shipping that link the atolls.

register.name: Pacific Islands Regional Oceanscape Program, second phase: Tuvalu
register.detail: World Bank · IDA grant · Approved 8 December 2023
register.note: The World Bank’s press release of December 2023 gives a US$13 million grant
register.text: A grant from the International Development Association for the second phase of the Pacific Islands Regional Oceanscape Program in Tuvalu, to strengthen fisheries policies and boost sustainable community-based resource management and protection. It aims to create new jobs and livelihoods in small-scale fishing and tuna-related services, which serves the food and livelihood standards.

register.name: First Climate and Disaster Resilience DPF with a Cat DDO
register.detail: World Bank · Grant · Approved 22 September 2023 · Development policy grant $7.5M and Cat DDO $4M
register.note: US$11.5 million (AU$18 million), according to the World Bank; followed by a second operation in March 2025
register.text: Budget support of US$7.5 million with a catastrophe deferred drawdown option of US$4 million, available immediately after a natural disaster. It protects public spending on the seven standards when disaster strikes.

register.name: Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project (FP015)
register.detail: Green Climate Fund · UNDP · Approved 30 June 2016 · Effective 7 June 2017 · GCF grant $36.01M, co-financing $2.86M · Completion date 7 December 2025
register.note: The disbursements the GCF lists, the last on 12 December 2024, add up to the full $36.01M; Australia has committed A$38 million to the project
register.text: A Green Climate Fund grant, through UNDP, to build coastal resilience on three of Tuvalu’s nine inhabited islands and protect 2,780 metres of high-value vulnerable coastline. Under the project’s second phase, eight hectares of new land have been reclaimed and raised on Fogafale, designed to remain above projected sea-level rise beyond 2100, according to UNDP. Safe, raised land for homes serves the shelter standard.

register.name: Pacific Regional Energy Security Emergency Assistance Project
register.detail: Asian Development Bank · Grant to Tuvalu · Announced 12 October 2026 · $40.1M in all for Kiribati, Tonga and Tuvalu
register.text: Emergency grant financing to help Tuvalu manage its exposure to fuel price volatility amid the crisis in the Middle East, with targeted assistance to around 6,000 people from low-income households. It protects the energy standard and household budgets when fuel prices rise.

register.name: Supporting Public Sector Management Reform Program
register.detail: Asian Development Bank · Policy-based grant from the Asian Development Fund · Announced 11 November 2025 · The program has two subprograms
register.note: Policy-based grants are paid into the government’s general budget once agreed reforms are completed
register.text: Budget support for reforms that strengthen public financial management for fiscal resilience, the transparency and accountability of public entities, and climate resilience, tied to Tuvalu’s national goal of relying entirely on renewable energy by 2030. Sounder public finances sustain spending on the seven standards.

register.name: Funafuti Water Supply and Sanitation Project
register.detail: Asian Development Bank · ADF grant · Grant agreement signed 19 November 2024 · With $4.59M from the GEF Least Developed Countries Fund, $4.3M from New Zealand and $0.3M from the Government of Tuvalu
register.note: In January to June 2026 the project was in its readiness phase, with no civil works under way, according to ADB
register.text: Grant financing for Tuvalu’s first reticulated water network, improving household access to desalinated water and resilience to drought, with better sanitation, upgraded school and health centre facilities and a sewage treatment plant. ADB says the network will benefit more than half of the country’s population. It serves the water standard, the furthest from reach in Tuvalu.

register.name: Batteries and electricity networks for Funafuti and the outer islands
register.detail: Asian Development Bank · ADF grant · Committed 2024 · With a $1.84M grant from the Global Environment Facility · Project 49450-015
register.note: ADB had committed $184 million to Tuvalu in all by 31 December 2025
register.text: Grant financing to replace end-of-life batteries and upgrade damaged electricity networks in Tuvalu’s outer islands and Funafuti. It serves the energy standard.

register.name: Australian development assistance, 2025–26
register.detail: Australian Government · Total ODA budget estimate 2025–26 · A$86.7M budget estimate 2024–25 · A$60.3M in 2023–24 · Bilateral A$26.0M in 2025–26
register.note: Australia’s education partnership with Tuvalu is A$10 million over 2022–27, according to DFAT
register.text: Australia’s total official development assistance to Tuvalu in its 2025–26 budget estimate. It supports the expansion of safe land under the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project, public financial management and essential government expenditure, medical specialists at Princess Margaret Hospital and the Tuvalu and Australia Partnership for Quality Education, which serve the shelter, health and education standards.
by: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

register.name: Australia–Tuvalu Falepili Union: immediate priorities
register.detail: Australian Government · Announced 9 May 2024 · Treaty in force from 28 August 2024 · A$50M undersea cable · A$19M more for coastal adaptation, A$38M in all · A$10M budget support · A$15M security coordination centre
register.note: More than A$110 million, according to the Australian Government; the treaty also opens a mobility pathway with 280 visas in its first year
register.text: The package of immediate priorities Australia announced under the Falepili Union, the treaty between the two nations that entered into force on 28 August 2024. It finances Tuvalu’s first undersea telecommunications cable, more safe land under the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project, budget support for critical services and a National Security Coordination Centre. The new land and the budget support serve the shelter standard and public spending on the seven standards.
by: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

register.name: New Zealand International Development Cooperation, 2024–27
register.detail: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade · Approved funding for 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2027 · Plan target for Tuvalu
register.note: New Zealand gave Tuvalu $2.4 million of grant cofinancing in 2025, according to ADB
register.text: New Zealand’s approved development cooperation for Tuvalu over the three years to June 2027. New Zealand also cofinances, with $4.3 million, the Funafuti Water Supply and Sanitation Project, which serves the water standard, the furthest from reach in Tuvalu.
by: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade
